title: Werpos
summary: A Brooklyn placename near Merechkawikingh, recorded in a 1640 Kieft patent and interpreted as a bushy place or thicket.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Marking the location of an Indigenous village that once stood near present-day Hoyt and Baltic Streets, the traditional place name Werpos grounds Native history directly within the modern Brooklyn grid. Reclaiming these older urban place names challenges the assumption that Indigenous communities only existed in rural spaces, reminding us that Native geography forms the foundation of our busiest cities.
history_content: The name appears in a Kieft patent for land on Long Island near Merechkawikingh. A later Schoolcraft comparison with a Manhattan locality is treated cautiously.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Werpos and Warpoes. Tooker rejects a rabbit-name explanation and instead suggests a connection with a word meaning a bushy place or thicket.

Why Place Names Matter

“Reinstating Indigenous place names plays an important role in recognizing, preserving, and strengthening Indigenous languages.”

— Canada's History, Lesson: Indigenous Place Names in Canada (2025), Background, PDF page 1, second paragraph
preservation_content: Werpos preserves an early Brooklyn locality name from the Dutch colonial record and connects the area with the wider Lenape place-name landscape around Merechkawikingh.

whereintheworld_content: The existing polygon near Hoyt and Baltic Streets remains the map reference; no separate point is needed for this polygon record.
